title: Navigation for a manufacturer
excerpt: Build the menu from buyer jobs, in words they already use, with one path to sales or a spec on every page. Department labels make them translate.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table, for a piece on navigation a buyer can use without a guide.
caption: One person, one laptop, one task. A menu should be that direct. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What labels belong in a manufacturer menu?
faqs.answer: The jobs a buyer already has. Find the object, see the process, open the spec, read a proof, talk to sales. Test a label by finishing the sentence 'I need to.' If it cannot, it is a drawer, and the thing inside the drawer should be promoted instead.

faqs.question: Should Quality be a top-level item?
faqs.answer: Usually no. Evidence of inspection belongs in the spec, the proof, and the about page, next to the work it covers. A badge gallery under a Quality label does not help someone judge a part. Sales can stay, because contacting sales is a job the buyer has.

faqs.question: How should the phone menu differ?
faqs.answer: It should use the same words and the same order. The difference is that the primary action, spec or sales, should stay visible when the menu is closed. Hiding that path inside the icon demotes it on the device many buyers actually use.

markdown:
Manufacturer website navigation is a map of jobs, for a buyer who needs specs and confidence. The labels should be words they already use. One path should talk to sales or download a spec, and that path should be available from every page. A menu that copies the company's departments tells the buyer how you are organized. It does not tell them how to find a part, a process, or a file.

Build the menu from tasks. Find the object. See how it is made. Check the spec. Judge a proof. Start a conversation. If a label does not serve one of those tasks, it has to earn its place some other way, and most of the time it cannot.

## Labels in the buyer's vocabulary

Sit with the phrases that show up in inquiries and on purchase orders. Housings, panels, kits, the process name, the spec, the industry only when buyers ask for it that way. Those phrases become the labels. Internal words, "solutions," "offerings," "capabilities center," "innovation," stay off the bar unless your buyers truly say them. Most do not.

Test a label by finishing the sentence "I need to…" If the label cannot finish that sentence for a stranger, rewrite it. "Products" works when you have products. "Download specs" works when a file exists. "Resources" rarely works, because it names a drawer, not a job. Open the drawer and promote the one or two files people actually need. Hide the rest in the footer or delete them.

Keep labels short and distinct. Two items that a buyer could confuse, "Capabilities" and "Services," "Work" and "Projects," should become one item. Synonyms in a menu are a tax on attention. Pick the word sales already uses on the phone and repeat it. The site, the spec, and the quote should share a vocabulary, and the menu is where a new buyer learns it.

Order the bar by the sequence of a buying decision. Object, process, spec, proof, then the action. Company information can sit at the end or in the footer. Leading with About, News, and Careers tells a buyer the site was arranged for the team. Leading with the object tells them it was arranged for the inquiry.

## One path that never disappears

The action, talk to sales or download a spec, belongs in the bar or immediately beside it on every page. If you offer both, choose a primary and keep the other one click away. A buyer who has seen enough should be able to act without returning to the homepage to hunt for a contact link buried under a paragraph.

Make the primary action look like an action. A text label among other text labels is easy to miss. A clear control, with a verb, is easier to trust. The verb should match the rest of the site. If the homepage says "Send a drawing," the nav should not say "Let's partner." Inconsistent verbs feel like inconsistent companies.

On inner pages, repeat the action in the page itself as well as in the nav. People who arrive from a search result or a forwarded link may never look at the bar. The nav is the persistent reminder. The page still has to carry its own next step. Navigation supports the offer. It does not replace the sentence on the page.

If the spec is public, "Specs" can be a direct link to the file or to a short index of files. Sending someone to a vague library page with twelve unlabeled PDFs is a broken path. Name the files the way the buyer names the products. Update the index when a revision ships. A nav item that leads to a stale file is worse than no item, because it looks official.

## What not to promote into the bar

Department names are the common mistake. Quality, Human Resources, Sales, Operations. Sales survives, because talking to sales is a job the buyer has. The others are internal. Quality's evidence belongs inside the spec, the proof, and the about page. A top-level Quality item that opens a badge gallery does not help a buyer judge a part.

News and blog posts should not outrank the spec. If you publish useful notes, put them where a curious buyer can find them, often the footer or a single "Notes" label. Do not let the newest post become the thing the header is shouting. The header has a job. It is the map. A campaign, a trade-show announcement, or a seasonal message can live in a small, dismissible line. It should not replace a permanent label.

Language and region selectors matter when you truly operate that way. A selector with one language, or a region list that all leads to the same page, is clutter. Add it when the second version exists. The same rule covers a login for customers. If a portal is real, link it plainly, and keep it visually secondary to the path for a new buyer. Existing customers know to look. New buyers should not have to decode a lock icon before they find a product.

## Menus, footers, and the pages underneath

A simple bar is better than a giant panel of every page you have ever made. If you need a second level, use it for real children. Products opens to the product families. Specs opens to the documents. Proof opens to three named jobs. A mega-menu full of marketing phrases, with no page that matches the phrase, trains people to ignore the menu.

The footer can hold the slow jobs. Address, employment, privacy, the long certification list, the archive of older notes. Put the plant address in text, not only inside a map image. Repeat the primary action once in the footer for people who scroll to the end of a proof looking for what to do. Do not invent a second, competing action down there.

Search on the site is optional at this size. A five-page site with a search box often has a navigation problem wearing a search costume. Add search when the spec library or the proof library is large enough that a menu cannot show it. Then make sure the search can find the spec by the buyer's noun. A search that only indexes blog adjectives will frustrate the person with a part number or a process name.

Breadcrumbs help on proof pages and deeper spec pages, so a visitor can see the parent. They are a minor aid. They do not fix a confusing bar. If you add them, use the same labels as the menu. A breadcrumb that says "Insights" while the menu says "Notes" is a small crack in an otherwise learnable map.

## The phone menu is the real menu

Many of these buyers will open the site on a phone, in a hallway or on a floor. The menu has to work there with a thumb, with labels that fit, and with the action still visible when the menu is closed. If the desktop bar contains eight items and the phone hides all eight behind an icon, including the path to sales, you have demoted the action at the moment it is most needed.

Keep the action outside the collapsed menu when you can. A persistent "Spec" or "Sales" control in the header, plus a menu for the rest, matches the way the page is actually used. Inside the menu, use the same order and the same words as the wide screen. A separate, shorter mobile information architecture surprises people who switch devices mid-task, which buyers do when they forward a page to a colleague.

Tap targets need space. A stacked list of labels with enough padding beats a clever grid of tiny icons. Icons without words are a guessing game. If you use an icon for the menu itself, the word "Menu" beside it removes doubt. The [W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes operable content as something people can navigate and use, including ways to find where they are and where they can go. A manufacturer menu meets that standard when the jobs are named in text, the order is stable, and the next step is present without a hunt.

## Check the map with people who buy

Before you freeze the labels, read them to someone who was not in the redesign meetings. A salesperson is a good first reader. A friendly customer is a better one, if you can ask without turning it into a workshop. Give them a task. "Where would you download the housing spec?" "Where would you send a drawing?" Watch where they go. Fix the label they hesitated on. Do not explain the logic and then keep the label. The hesitation is the result.

Do the same with a page that arrives from outside. Open a proof link directly and ask how they would reach the spec from there. Navigation fails in these cross-links more often than it fails on the homepage, because the homepage was the only screen anyone reviewed. Click every item. Make sure the destination's heading matches the label that pointed at it. "Products" should not land on a manifesto.

Write the menu down as a simple list in the project notes. When someone later asks to add "Sustainability" or "Community" to the bar, you can ask which job it serves for a buyer with a drawing. Sometimes the honest answer is a footer link to a single page. Sometimes the honest answer is not yet. The bar stays short because the buyer's job stayed the same.

Hanabi builds these maps as part of the site, in the same pass as the pages, so the labels and the headings agree. You can see the bias toward a readable public site in [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The relevant lesson is structural. A visitor can tell what the organization offers and where to go next, without learning an internal dialect.

The labels will point at photographs as much as at sentences. Those pictures are part of the argument a buyer is judging. [Photography direction for a manufacturer](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-manufacturer) is the next piece, because the frames have to show the object and how it is made, and a factory cliché with no product will undo a clear menu.
